scenes.title: Kafka vs Traditional Message Queues
scenes.subtitle: Log-based streaming versus classic queuing
scenes.narration: Kafka and traditional message queues both move messages, but they differ fundamentally in how they store and deliver them.

scenes.title: How They Differ at the Core
bullets: Queues delete a message once acknowledged
Kafka retains messages for a whole retention window
Queues push to one consumer; Kafka lets many groups read
Kafka replays history; queues generally cannot
scenes.narration: A traditional queue typically deletes a message as soon as one consumer acknowledges it. Kafka instead retains every message for its full retention window, regardless of who has read it. Queues usually hand each message to a single consumer, whereas Kafka lets many independent consumer groups read the same stream. And because the log persists, Kafka can replay history, something classic queues generally cannot do.

scenes.title: When to Use Which
scenes.narration: A traditional broker like RabbitMQ shines at task distribution, complex routing rules, and per-message features such as priorities and time-to-live. Kafka shines when you need high-throughput event streams, many independent consumers of the same data, and the ability to replay events. Choosing between them comes down to whether you need transient work distribution or a durable event backbone.

scenes.title: The Consumption Difference
steps: Queue: consumer takes and it is gone
New consumers can start from the past
scenes.narration: Picture a single message being published. In a queue, a consumer takes it and the message disappears from the broker. In Kafka, the consumer simply advances its offset while the message remains on disk. That difference means a brand new consumer group can join later and start reading from the very beginning.

scenes.text: Kafka is a durable, replayable log, not just a queue. Reach for it when many systems must share the same events over time.
scenes.narration: The bottom line is that Kafka is a durable, replayable log, not just a queue. Reach for it when many systems must share the same events over time.
